city_metadata.title: EXPLAINOPOLIS
city_metadata.subtitle: A map that explains how it was made · metropolis-kit + deckcast
city_metadata.scale_axis_description: South to north: a document nobody reads → agents that understand it → a compiler that builds views → voices that tell it → maps already in use.

districts.name: 1 · THE DOCUMENT
districts.description: Real sources that were explained with this kit: a report chapter, a research paper, a project canvas.

districts.name: 2 · UNDERSTANDING
districts.description: Two agents turn a document into a one-page profile and then a semantic spec; a person approves both and a provenance file keeps every number honest.

districts.name: 3 · BUILDING
districts.description: A deterministic compiler turns the spec into a 3D city, a metro map and a guided tour.

districts.name: 4 · VOICE
districts.description: deckcast voices the tour as a dialogue; then pre-voiced questions; then a live agent that answers and moves the map.

districts.name: 5 · IN USE
districts.description: Maps and narrated decks that exist today.

spires.title: SCIANCE D1.1 — Materials Science chapter
spires.abstract: A landscape report chapter on AI in European materials science, revised three times while the map followed it. The kind of document reviewers skim and nobody reads to page 47.

spires.title: arXiv:2609.11975 — AI-Research Agents in the Wild
spires.abstract: A meta-study of the public ecosystem of AI-research agents, with six candidate regularities, a prospective audit and three supplementary tables. Its argument lives in tables and caveats.

spires.title: Knowledge Discovery — CEO status canvas

metrics.maturity: Explained in a private CEO map

spires.abstract: A project status canvas: epics, waiting items, a risk cascade and milestones. A different kind of document — a plan, not a text — explained with the same kit.

spires.title: Discovery agent

metrics.acceleration: Reads the source, proposes the metaphor

spires.abstract: Reads the source document and proposes the city: the axis, the districts, the landmarks, the bottlenecks, the flows. Output is a short domain profile a human can review in minutes.

spires.title: Domain profile
spires.abstract: The first gate: one page that states how the document will be mapped and why. Cheap to argue about before anything is built.

spires.title: Architect agent
spires.abstract: Turns the approved profile into a city spec: stations, flows, constraints, priorities, tour — with no coordinates. Rules in the prompt: numbers only from the source, constraints placed where they act.

spires.title: City spec

metrics.acceleration: Districts · spires · roads · constraints · tour · metro

spires.abstract: The contract between understanding and building. Pure semantics — what exists, what flows where, what blocks what, what the tour says — and every view and every voice is generated from it.

spires.title: Human review & provenance

metrics.acceleration: Paper vs derived vs map choice

spires.abstract: A person approves the profile and the spec, and a provenance file separates what the source says, what was recounted, and what is a choice of the map. It caught a claim in the paper that its own data do not support.

spires.title: Spatial compiler
spires.abstract: Deterministic: validates references, places buildings, routes roads, derives traffic, queues, weather, the metro layout and the tour cameras. No coordinates are ever written by hand unless asked.

spires.title: City view
spires.abstract: Districts, buildings whose shape says what a thing is, roads with traffic and barriers, data tables painted on the ground.

spires.title: Metro view

metrics.scale: SVG schematic from the same spec

spires.abstract: For readers who find the city too busy: the same spec as a metro map — lines per district, compact interchanges with an explanation card, labels that never overlap.

spires.title: Guided tour

metrics.maturity: Nine stops in the paper map

spires.abstract: A story told with the map: each stop flies the camera, dims everything else and says one thing. The stops are what the voices will read.

spires.title: Validator & render checks
spires.abstract: Refuses a spec with broken references or impossible combinations, and every change is checked by rendering it headless before it ships.

spires.title: deckcast
spires.abstract: Compiles a narration script into voiced clips with a cache, measures them and builds a timeline — a video, or per-page audio with line-level cues for a web player.

spires.title: Narration script
spires.abstract: The handover between the map and the voices: one page per tour stop, one line per spoken sentence, two speakers.

spires.title: Audio & cues

metrics.scale: One mp3 per stop + line timings

spires.abstract: Lets the player show subtitles and fire map actions exactly when a line is spoken.

spires.title: Level 1 — narrated dialogue tour

metrics.acceleration: Lines move the map on cue

spires.abstract: The tour read as a conversation: the sceptic asks what a reviewer would ask, the guide answers and points at the map.

spires.title: Level 2 — the map asks

metrics.acceleration: Answer = a click on the map

spires.abstract: After a stop the sceptic asks a question; the reader answers by clicking on the map, and a recorded line says right or wrong and shows the answer.

spires.title: Level 3 — talk to the city

metrics.acceleration: Answers from the map, points with the tour's actions
metrics.infrastructure: knowledge base exported by the compiler

spires.abstract: Ask anything by voice; the agent answers from the map's own knowledge and flies the camera to the evidence.

spires.title: SCIANCE materials map
spires.abstract: The materials-science chapter as a city with constraints drawn where they act.

spires.title: Autoresearch in the Wild
spires.abstract: The paper as five story districts with lineages, failure modes, six rules on trial, data plazas and a provenance file.

spires.title: Knowledge Discovery CEO view
spires.abstract: A project as a time corridor with a 'you are here' line; kept private because it names people and risks.

spires.title: deckcast narrated decks
spires.abstract: Two decks already narrated end to end, one with a talk-to-the-agent link.

bottlenecks.title: A person must check the spec
bottlenecks.impact: Agents draft the profile and the spec, but numbers and claims need a human read before publishing; the paper map's provenance file exists for that reason.
bottlenecks.remedy: Keep the two gates and the provenance file; make the review a checklist.

bottlenecks.title: Dense maps need manual placement
bottlenecks.impact: Automatic placement handles small districts; districts with many buildings or plazas still need explicit positions in the spec.
bottlenecks.remedy: Smarter packing in the compiler; label placement already avoids overlaps.

bottlenecks.title: Dialogue is still written, not generated
bottlenecks.impact: The compiler exports the tour as a two-voice script and deckcast voices it, but someone still writes the dialogue lines in the spec.
bottlenecks.remedy: Draft the dialogue with the architect agent, then review it like the spec.

bottlenecks.title: The live agent needs the network
bottlenecks.impact: A live voice agent adds latency and can be unreachable during a demo.
bottlenecks.remedy: Levels 1 and 2 work offline from files; the mic button hides itself when the agent is unreachable.

challenges.title: Minutes, not pages
challenges.target: Understand a 50-page document's argument in a five-minute guided tour — and still be able to open every number.

challenges.title: Every number traceable
challenges.target: Each station says where its numbers come from: the source, a recount, or a choice of the map.

challenges.title: One spec, every view
challenges.target: City, metro, tour and voices are all generated from the same spec, so they never disagree.

challenges.title: Ask the city
challenges.target: Anyone can ask a question by voice and be shown the answer on the map.

plazas.title: From document to map

layers.label: Three real sources and the maps compiled from them

plazas.description: Three different kinds of source — a report chapter, a research paper, a project canvas — compiled by the same kit. Numbers are from the specs in this repository.

interchanges.label: Source

interchanges.label: The spec

interchanges.text: Everything downstream is compiled from this one file: the city, the metro, the tour, and the narration script.

sceptic.name: Owen
sceptic.role: sceptic — asks what a reviewer would ask

tour.title: Nobody reads page 47
tour.text: Reports, papers and project plans carry their argument in tables, caveats and page 47. These three were real, and each became a map.
tour.look: The three sources and the 'from document to map' plaza

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [warm] Welcome to Explainopolis — a map that explains how it was made. I'm Maya, I'll be your guide.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [dryly] And I'm Owen. I'll ask what you would ask. So — why a map? What's wrong with the document?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [thoughtful] Nothing, except that nobody reads it. A report keeps its argument in tables, caveats and page forty-seven. These three are real: a materials-science chapter, an arXiv paper, and a CEO's project canvas.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [skeptical] Three very different documents. One tool for all of them?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [confident] The same kit. This plaza is the evidence. The paper ran to about twenty-three thousand words; its map has thirty-eight buildings and a nine-stop tour.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [dryly] The goal out there says minutes, not pages. Let's see you earn it.

tour.title: Agents read, a human approves
tour.text: One agent proposes a one-page profile, another writes the spec. A person approves both, and a provenance file says where each number comes from.
tour.look: Discovery → profile → architect → spec, and the review gate

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [skeptical] Let me guess. You paste the paper into a chatbot and it draws a city?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [amused] Not quite. A discovery agent reads the source and proposes how to map it — the axis, the districts, the landmarks — on a single page.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: And who checks that page?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [matter-of-fact] A person. That's the first gate, and it's cheap: you argue about one page before anything is built. Then an architect agent turns the approved profile into a city spec — what exists, what flows where, what blocks what. No coordinates.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [pointed] Agents write numbers. Agents get numbers wrong.

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [serious] Which is why the second gate is here: a human review, and a provenance file that separates what the source says, what we recounted, and what is only a choice of the map. On the paper's map it records the one place where the map follows the authors' own audit instead of the printed text.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [dryly] So that red flag on the spec is a limit you admit, not a bug you hide.

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [warm] Exactly. Every map here draws its limits where they act.

ask.speaker: sceptic
ask.text: [dryly] Your turn. Show me where a human checks the agents' work.

right.speaker: guide
right.text: [pleased] Exactly. Agents draft, a person approves, and the provenance file keeps the receipts.

wrong.speaker: guide
wrong.text: [gentle] Close. The gates are here: the one-page profile, and the human review with its provenance file.

tour.title: One spec, many views
tour.text: A deterministic compiler turns the spec into a 3D city, a metro map and this tour. Change the spec, rebuild, and every view agrees.

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [brisk] From here on, nothing is guessed. The compiler reads the spec, places every building, routes every road, and works out the cameras for this tour.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [skeptical] Deterministic? Same spec, same city?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [confident] Same spec, same city. About fifteen hundred lines of plain Python. It refuses a spec with a broken reference, and every change is rendered headless before it ships.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [honest] Still, this city is a lot. I'd lose my manager by district two.

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [playful] Then switch. Same spec, drawn as a metro map: one line per district, and the interchanges are where the story changes lines.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [surprised] The same file? Not a second drawing?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [matter-of-fact] The same file. Click an interchange and it tells you why it's there. One spec, every view — that's the goal of this district.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [dryly] And the catch?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [candid] Big districts still need positions by hand. It's marked, right there on the compiler.

tour.title: The map talks — and listens
tour.text: deckcast voices the script with two speakers. The tour is a dialogue, the map asks you a question, and a live agent answers yours.
tour.look: deckcast, the handover files, and three levels of voice

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [dryly] Here's my real question. Who is talking right now?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [amused] We are — but neither of us was recorded. This conversation is a script in the same spec, and deckcast turned it into voices.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [curious] deckcast being?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [brisk] A small tool that compiles a narration script into voiced clips, caches them, and times every line. Those timings are why the map moves exactly when I say — here.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [impressed, grudging] Neat. So this tour is level one. What are two and three?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [excited] Level two: the map asks you — you've met it already — and you answer with a click. Level three: you simply ask, out loud, and an agent answers from the map's own knowledge and flies the camera for you.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [skeptical] A live agent in a live demo. What could possibly go wrong.

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [candid] The network. That's why it's marked as a limit — and why levels one and two need no live connection at all.

tour.title: Already working
tour.text: Two public maps, a private CEO view and two narrated decks exist today — and this map was built the same way.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [serious] Last question, and it's the one a jury asks. Is anyone actually using this?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [confident] Yes. The materials-science chapter and the arXiv paper are public maps you can open today.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: And the third one?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [matter-of-fact] A CEO's view of a live project. Private, because it names people and risks — same kit, kept local.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: And deckcast?

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: Two decks narrated end to end, one with a link where you can talk to the agent.

dialogue.speaker: sceptic
dialogue.text: [warmer] So the thing explaining itself is built exactly like the things it explains.

dialogue.speaker: guide
dialogue.text: [warm] That's the point. One spec, a compiler and a script — and a document nobody reads becomes a place you can walk through. And a place you can ask: press the Ask button, bottom right, and talk to me.
